key: An LLM judge is a measuring instrument

text: Like any instrument it has a design (what it is asked and how), known systematic errors (biases), a calibration against a reference (human labels), and a reliability that depends on whether you read one value or an average of many.
label: fat

text: This page goes through each in that order, with the evidence for every default.

text: Who judges whom A judge from another family, or a jury When humans preferred the other answer, the GPT-4 judge still gave the win to GPT-4 in 63% of those comparisons; for Claude-v1 the same figure is 29% ( Calibration lab ; confounded with GPT-4 simply being stronger).

text: Judge design: four modes A judge prompt fixes what is compared with what.
label: fat

text: Four modes cover nearly all practice, and each has its own failure.
label: fat

text: Pointwise (direct scoring) The judge sees one answer and returns a score: pass/fail, 1 to 5 against a rubric, or MT-Bench's 1 to 10.
label: core

text: It needs no baseline, so it suits monitoring and regression gates, and it costs one call per answer.
label: core

text: Its weakness is the scale itself: a 7 means whatever this judge, this prompt and this week's model version make it mean, so scores from different judge versions are not comparable.
label: core

text: Two fixes are standard.
label: fat

text: Anchor few levels : binary pass/fail with a written critique is Hamel Husain's default because "a binary decision forces everyone to consider what truly matters" ( Creating an LLM-as-a-Judge ); the old page's "fine scales are noise past about 4 distinguishable levels" has no source this page could find ( unconfirmed ).
label: core

text: Read the distribution, not the sampled token : G-Eval asks for a 1 to 5 score after chain-of-thought evaluation steps and takes the probability-weighted sum of the score tokens, reaching Spearman 0.514 with humans on summarisation ( Liu et al.
label: core

text: 2023 ); RocketEval reads P(Yes)/(P(Yes)+P(No)) for each checklist item.
label: core

text: Pairwise (preference) The judge sees two answers and picks one, or a tie.
label: core

text: People find comparisons easier than absolute scores, and "is the new model better than the old one" is a comparison.
label: core

text: It carries position bias (so both orders are run), tie handling (a tie option and order disagreements both produce ties, and agreement figures change with how they are counted), and cost: ranking n systems by all pairs takes n(n−1)/2 comparisons per prompt, twice that with both orders, so leaderboards compare every system against one baseline instead (MT-Bench pairwise, AlpacaEval, Arena-Hard).
label: core

text: Pairwise is also more exposed to distractors: when generators embedded features the judge likes, pairwise preferences flipped in about 35% of cases against 9% for absolute scores ( Tripathi et al.
label: core

text: On MT-Bench neither mode wins.
label: core

text: Checklist and rubric decomposition Instead of one holistic judgment, the question is compiled into small yes/no checks, each answered separately and aggregated by a program.
label: core

text: RocketEval has a frontier model write each query's checklist once, then lets a small model answer each item and reads the probability of "Yes" ( RocketEval paper page ); RubricEval rates judges at the level of single rubric items and found rubric-level grading beat checklist-level, with GPT-4o at 55.97% on its Hard subset (atlas row RubricEval; preprint).
label: core

text: Decomposition says which criterion failed, removes the channel through which one answer's order or length leaks into the grade, and lets a small model do the grading.

text: Calibration against human gold No judge number means anything until it has been checked against human labels on the same kind of data.
label: core

text: Calibration answers three questions in turn: how often does the judge agree with people, corrected for chance; what are its error rates on each class; and what does its pass rate become once those errors are corrected.
label: core

text: Building the gold slice: Critique Shadowing Hamel Husain's method ( Creating an LLM-as-a-Judge That Drives Business Results, 29 Oct 2024 ), as the post reads in October 2026: One principal domain expert (a psychologist for a mental-health assistant, a lawyer for legal analysis) decides what is acceptable.
label: depth

text: A dataset spanning the product's features, scenarios and personas, with real system outputs (synthetic user inputs are fine).
label: depth

text: The expert gives each output pass or fail with a written critique , detailed enough that a new employee could follow the reasoning.
label: depth

text: No 1 to 5 scales.
label: depth

text: Fix the obvious system failures the review turns up before building any judge.
label: depth

text: Build the judge from the expert's critiques as few-shot examples and iterate the prompt until judge and expert agree; in the post's Honeycomb example this reached ">90% agreement" in three iterations.
label: depth

text: Error analysis by root cause; about 100 labelled examples per failure mode to validate a judge ("Below 60 examples, the confidence intervals are often too wide").
label: depth

text: Specialised judges only where the analysis shows a recurring failure.
label: depth

text: The post asks for the judge's true positive rate and true negative rate separately rather than raw agreement, because "agreement can be misleading when failures are rare", and splits the labelled data about 10 to 20% for few-shot examples and 40 to 45% each for development and test.

text: Those two rates are exactly what the correction below needs.

text: Agreement, corrected for chance Raw agreement flatters a judge whenever one label dominates.
label: core

text: Cohen's kappa subtracts the agreement two raters would reach by chance given how often each uses each label: κ = (p o − p e ) / (1 − p e ).
label: core

text: On MT-Bench, GPT-4's 66.2% agreement with the 3,355 votes is κ = 0.337, and across 21 judges in 2026 raw agreement overstated kappa by 33 to 41 points on MT-Bench ( Norman et al. ).
label: core

text: The parent page's Calibration section works the formula on an example and charts the human ceiling: two MT-Bench experts agree 63% with ties and 81% without, so a judge near those figures is at the ceiling of the labels, not below it.
label: core

text: Correcting the pass rate A judge with errors reports a biased pass rate even when its agreement looks fine.
label: core

text: Call the true pass rate θ, the judge's pass rate p, its sensitivity q 1 (the share of truly passing items it passes) and its specificity q 0 (the share of truly failing items it fails).
label: core

text: Then p = q 1 θ + (1 − q 0 )(1 − θ), which inverts to the Rogan-Gladen estimator (1978), used for LLM judges by Lee et al. (arXiv 2511.21140, v4 May 2026) : θ̂ = (p̂ + q̂ 0 − 1) / (q̂ 0 + q̂ 1 − 1) p̂ the judge's pass rate on all n test items q̂ 1 , q̂ 0 the judge's sensitivity and specificity measured on a human-labelled gold slice of m 1 passing and m 0 failing items interval the paper's eq.
label: core

text: 8: an adjusted Wald interval (add two successes and two failures to each rate) whose variance adds the test-set term p(1−p)/n and the two calibration terms (1−θ)²q 0 (1−q 0 )/m 0 and θ²q 1 (1−q 1 )/m 1 , all divided by (q 0 +q 1 −1)², truncated to [0, 1] The denominator is the whole story.
label: core

text: A judge with q 0 + q 1 near 1 carries almost no information about the truth, and the correction then divides noise by a small number.
label: core

text: Three results from the paper matter in practice.

text: The estimator stays unbiased when the gold slice and the test set have different pass rates, as long as the judge's error rates are the same on both, which is not true of the prediction-powered alternatives.

label: core

text: Reliability is not validity A judge can repeat itself perfectly and be systematically wrong.
label: core

text: Norman et al. found test-retest reliability above 0.95 together with position bias above 0.10 in two production judges (Qwen 3 8B: 0.992 and 0.192, with JudgeBench kappa 0.289; Gemini 2.5 Flash: 0.988 and 0.125), because a judge that always prefers slot A is perfectly reproducible.
label: core

text: Their minimum validation protocol before deploying a judge: Chance-correct: report Cohen's kappa (or Krippendorff's alpha) as the headline, beside any raw agreement.
label: core

text: Swap positions: run AB and BA and report |P(A wins) − 0.5|.
label: core

text: Replicate: at least 3 runs at temperature 0 with response caching off.
label: core

text: Cross-validate: at least 2 meta-evaluations, one preference-style and one correctness-style.
label: core

text: Audit the paradox: when test-retest is above 0.95, check that position bias is below 0.10 before calling the judge reliable.
label: core

text: Juries and robust aggregation PoLL ( Verga et al.
label: core

text: 2024 ) replaces one large judge with three smaller ones from disjoint families (Command R, Claude 3 Haiku, GPT-3.5), each judging independently.
label: core

text: Binary correctness verdicts are pooled by majority ("max voting"); Arena-style 1 to 5 scores by their average, because three judges often produce no majority.
label: core

text: On KILT Natural Questions answers the panel reached kappa 0.763 with human labels against 0.627 for GPT-4 alone (exact string match: 0.651; Claude 3 Haiku alone: 0.749), and its model ranking correlated with Chatbot Arena at Pearson 0.917 against 0.817, "while being over seven times less expensive".
label: core

text: The evidence is the authors' own, on question answering with references and Arena-Hard, and the best single small judge came within 0.014 kappa of the panel: much of the gain over GPT-4 is GPT-4 doing worse on this task, not pooling.
label: core

text: Why the mean is fragile.
label: core

text: RoPoLL (Acharya et al., arXiv 2606.30931, June 2026, preprint) models a jury under Huber contamination and proves that mean pooling "incurs unbounded bias under any positive contamination, regardless of jury size, whenever a single judge fails in a biased, LLM-typical way (mode collapse, sycophancy, safety refusal)".
label: core

text: It swaps the mean for the geometric median (computed by a modified Weiszfeld iteration), which needs no tuning, keeps the scores' joint structure, and tolerates up to half the jurors failing.
label: core

text: Across 13 open-weight judges (4B to 675B), three reward-model benchmarks and corruption rates up to 50%, it beat mean pooling on every biased corruption type, by about 19% on cross-dimensional attacks; a 3-judge committee totalling 38B beat Mistral-Large-3 (675B) by 1.31x on HelpSteer-2 under 30% bimodal corruption.
label: depth

text: Under benign Gaussian noise the mean remains the statistically optimal choice, so the median buys insurance, not accuracy.
label: core

text: Practical form: median or trimmed mean over jurors, plus per-juror agreement tracked over time so a degraded juror is noticed.
label: core

text: Debate and meta-judges (agents argue, or a judge adjudicates juror disagreement) are expensive and not reliably better.
label: core

text: On JudgeBench, ChatEval's multi-agent debate with GPT-4o scored 34.0%, against 56.57% for one GPT-4o with the Arena-Hard prompt (atlas, JudgeBench v1 Table 1).
label: core

text: Keep them for offline audits where a disagreement needs a written argument.
label: core

text: Escalation spends the judge budget where the signal is: a cheap jury on everything; items where jurors disagree, or scores near the threshold, go to a stronger judge; items where that judge and the jury still disagree go to a person.
label: core

text: The escalated items are also the most useful additions to the gold slice.
